source: NASA Mars Exploration Program, Mars Relay Network Handbook, JPL D-71874, Release 4 (April 27, 2026), Table 2-3 and sections 3.1, 3.3, 5.2. https://assets.science.nasa.gov/content/dam/science/psd/mars/files/mars-relay-network/MRN%20Handbook_v4_final_URS_cleared.pdf
use: When the astronaut can talk to Earth through Perseverance. The rover sends to an orbiter over UHF during a pass; the orbiter forwards to Earth later, and the signal then takes the one-way light time (reference.json mars.lightTimeOneWayMin). A reply comes up the same way on a later pass.

orbiters.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (NASA)
orbiters.passesPerSol: at least 2 at low latitudes (Jezero is 18.4 N)
orbiters.note: Short 7-8 min overflights are not usually used; 10-11 min is typical for the passes that are.

orbiters.name: 2001 Mars Odyssey (NASA)
orbiters.passesPerSol: 2-4 within 30 deg of the equator, clustered around the two node times

orbiters.name: ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA)
orbiters.orbit: low, 76 deg inclination, not Sun-synchronous, so pass times drift from week to week
orbiters.note: A typical TGO session with adaptive data rate lasts about 17 minutes.

orbiters.name: Mars Express (ESA)
orbiters.note: Highly elliptical orbit: less frequent passes with widely varying range.

notMoreAvailable.MAVEN: Lost in 2025 (handbook section 1). Do not list it as a current relay.

gameWindowsLTST.about: Simple schedule for the game: the two Sun-synchronous orbiters pass Jezero near fixed local times. Windows are node time +/- 1 h because the nearest ground track can fall either side of the site. Times are LMST; the game clock is LTST, which differs by up to about 50 minutes over the Mars year, so treat the windows as approximate. TGO adds about one pass at a varying time.
gameWindowsLTST.values: Window width and the one-pass-per-window rule are design simplifications; node times and pass lengths are from the handbook.
